# Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering

Also called: Fourier window, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zero-order interpolation, Zeroth-order interpolation, box filter

## Overview
Interpolation schemes for volume rendering approximate a continuous scalar field $V(\mathbf{p})$ from discrete voxel samples $V_i$ to determine values at arbitrary query positions $\mathbf{p}$ along viewing rays [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. The choice of scheme dictates the trade-off between computational cost and visual fidelity, ranging from the blocky, artifact-prone nearest-neighbor method to high-quality, computationally expensive higher-order filters like tri-cubic B-splines or windowed sinc functions [S4, S5, unofficial]. Unlike [Interpolation Methods](10526-interpolation-methods.md) which covers general mathematical techniques, this family focuses on reconstruction filters specifically optimized for volumetric data, including frequency-domain resampling and hardware-accelerated approximations.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function $V(\mathbf{p})$ must be approximated from a discrete set of samples $V_i$ located at grid positions $\mathbf{p}_i$. The core mechanism involves:

1.  **Query Positioning**: Determining the 3D coordinate $\mathbf{p}$ along the ray $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ where a value is needed. This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings.
2.  **Kernel/Weight Application**: Computing weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$ based on the distance between $\mathbf{p}$ and the sample centers $\mathbf{p}_i$. The interpolated value is:
    $$
    V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i
    $$
    The choice of kernel (e.g., linear, cubic, inverse distance) determines the spatial extent (number of neighbors) and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].
3.  **Coordinate Transformation**: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized $[-1, 1]$ or $[0, 1]$ ranges) before interpolation .

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)
Frequency Domain Volume Rendering (FD method) is a direct volume rendering technique that performs resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using Fourier transforms to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors. It exploits signal processing principles such as the shifting, packing, and derivative theorems to achieve the best theoretical reconstruction quality using the ideal sinc filter. Unlike standard spatial domain methods (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or hybrid approaches that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples volume slices in object space via zero-padding, ensuring superior accuracy for high-magnification views.

### [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md)
Fast tri-cubic interpolation is a GPU-based reconstruction technique that evaluates a tri-cubic B-spline filter using only eight tri-linear texture fetches, significantly reducing the computational cost compared to the standard 64 nearest-neighbor fetches required for a full tri-cubic convolution. It sets itself apart from standard tri-cubic interpolation by leveraging the linear filtering capabilities of GPU texture units and the separability of tensor-product B-splines to combine weighted sums into fewer hardware operations. Unlike [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md) or [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md), it provides higher-order continuity ($C^2$) and smoother results, while avoiding the high memory bandwidth cost of naive cubic sampling.

### [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md)
Bilinear interpolation is a reconstruction scheme that estimates values at arbitrary 2D coordinates by performing linear interpolation in both spatial dimensions. It solves the problem of sampling discrete grid data (such as textures, scalar fields, or feature maps) at non-integer positions, providing a smoother result than nearest-neighbor interpolation while remaining computationally inexpensive. It sets itself apart from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) by operating on 2D planes rather than 3D volumes, and from [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md) by using a local linear kernel rather than a global sinc function, trading frequency accuracy for speed.

### [Hardware Interpolation Approximation](1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md)
Hardware Interpolation Approximation is a volume rendering technique that leverages graphics hardware rasterization to approximate the volume rendering integral. It solves the problem of efficient ray casting by mapping the integration process to polygon subdivision and hardware-driven linear interpolation. It is distinct from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) and [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md) because the interpolation kernel is not fixed to the volume grid but is instead determined by the geometric subdivision of the view plane polygons by the graphics pipeline.

### [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md)
Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values of the 8 surrounding voxels, based on their distances to the sample point. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling by providing a continuous, first-order approximation of the underlying scalar field. It produces softer, higher-quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but requires approximately 5 times more computation time.

### [Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation](2336-inverse-distance-weighted-interpolation.md)
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that estimates the value of a continuous scalar field at a query point by computing a weighted average of nearby sample values, where the influence of each sample decreases as its distance from the query point increases. It is chosen when a smooth, non-linear reconstruction is required from sparse or irregular data points (such as drill-hole assays) and when the computational cost of higher-order schemes like tri-linear or tri-cubic interpolation is prohibitive or when the underlying data structure is not a regular grid. Unlike [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md), which assumes a regular grid and guarantees $C^0$ continuity along interior faces, IDW is grid-agnostic and does not guarantee continuity across cell boundaries unless extended to neighboring cells.

### Variable Gaussian Blurring
A reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit [S6, unofficial]. It involves applying variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images [S6, unofficial]. The Nyquist limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts [S6, unofficial].

### Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels
Interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center [S7, unofficial]. The color $c$ is calculated as $c = c_1 \frac{A_2}{A} + c_2 \frac{A_3}{A} + c_3 \frac{A_1}{A}$, where $A_1 = \text{area}(v_1, v_2, P)$, $A_2 = \text{area}(v_2, v_3, P)$, $A_3 = \text{area}(v_3, v_1, P)$, $A = A_1 + A_2 + A_3$, and $P$ is the voxel center [S7, unofficial].

### Adaptive Interpolation for Isosurface Detection
Interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate. It uses non-binary classifiers to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate [S3, unofficial]. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used for the isovalue surface. When data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface [S3, unofficial]. This method supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor for preview, linear for day-to-day, and cubic for publication-quality [S3, unofficial].

### Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling
Resampling filters applied to extracted projection-slices to control ghosting artifacts and rendering quality during Fourier volume rendering [S8]. Point-sampling (nearest-neighbour) filters clamp missing samples to the nearest available value, causing apparent ghosting artifacts when the volume is rotated [S8]. Trilinear interpolation reduces replica intensities and ghosting artifacts compared to point-sampling, with similar performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$ but higher cost for larger volumes [S8]. A Hamming windowed-sinc interpolation filter with width 5 is a high-order reconstruction filter that maximally reduces ghosting artifacts when combined with zero-padding [S8]. Point-sampling and trilinear interpolation have nearly identical performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$, but trilinear incurs higher performance overhead for larger volumes [S8].

## Background
The simplest and fastest interpolation method for volume reconstruction is nearest-neighbor interpolation, which assigns the closest neighboring voxel value to a resample position [S1, unofficial]. It is also known as zero-order interpolation or sample-and-hold, resulting in a box filter [S2, unofficial]. In the spatial domain, this is equivalent to convolving the input signal with a one-sample-wide rect function (Fourier window) [S3, unofficial]. The rect function is defined as:
$$
h(\mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } |\mathbf{z}| < 0.5; \\ 0, & \text{if } |\mathbf{z}| = 0.5; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
$$
Convolution with the rect function in the spatial domain is equivalent to multiplication by the sinc function in the frequency domain [S3, unofficial]. However, the spatial rect function is a poor low-pass filter because the central lobe distorts the passband and the other lobes allow stopband energy to get through, causing aliasing [S3, unofficial]. Consequently, nearest-neighbor interpolation produces jagged edges, unpleasant staircasing, and blockiness, giving the poorest visual results [S2, S3, unofficial]. It is typically used only for quick-preview images [S3, unofficial].

Trilinear interpolation, the 3D version of bilinear interpolation, eliminates the artifacts present in nearest-neighbor interpolation by assuming a linear relation between neighboring voxels [S4, unofficial]. In 3D, it requires eight interpolation points [S1, unofficial]. While superior to nearest-neighbor, trilinear interpolation can exhibit three-dimensional cross (diamond) artifacts when using large magnification factors [S1, unofficial].

Higher-order interpolation schemes, such as tri-cubic interpolation using a cubic B-spline filter or windowed sinc filter, are used to improve rendering quality [S4, unofficial]. Tri-cubic interpolation takes 64 nearest samples and provides much better quality, though at considerably higher computational cost [S1, unofficial]. A common implementation uses a tri-cubic B-spline reconstruction filter, often with a Blackman window of width four for windowed sinc filters [S4, S5, unofficial]. These higher-order schemes are preferred for publication-quality imagery [S3, unofficial].
